cases.note: KP-028 is a descriptive note about the file formats KeePass uses or exports, not a requirement, so it gives a developer no instruction that could clash with the .kdb rules in KP-003/KP-021.
'Periodic' gives no interval or schedule, so backup frequency cannot be implemented consistently or tested (the 'will' wording is a minor extra).
The rule that these fields are read-only in a TAN entry is clear and testable, TAN is an established KeePass concept, and how the UI enforces it is a design choice.
KP-029 is an informational statement about what file formats are, not an instruction to the system, so vague wording in it has no effect on development.
KP-020 in the same document places sequences in the note field, and a sequence without the prefix is plainly not treated as an auto-type sequence, so a developer is unlikely to misread it.
The text only requires the password to be 'entered', not to be correct, and says nothing about the wrong-password case, which is the case that matters for a security behaviour.
The flagged phrase sits in the rationale sentence; the actual requirement ('Must use a SQL based database') is clear, so vagueness in the justification changes nothing.
'Policies are in place' names neither the policies, their content, nor who applies them, so the requirement cannot be implemented or verified.
The trailing words are a section heading merged into REQ-18 during extraction; the requirement itself is unambiguous, and the heading is not part of what is required.
REQ-18 just states a precondition (no connection means no download), and the claim wrongly reads the merged heading as evidence that use cases are missing.
The intent is clear: the confirmation field must match the new password before it is accepted, and the exact moment the check runs is a UI design detail.
It does not say which renegotiation policies, who runs them, or what triggers them, so the statement cannot be verified.
Saying the protocol 'is defined' without giving or referencing its content leaves the requirement incomplete and untestable, although the main gap is the missing content, not the missing actor.
The service-description format is neither given nor referenced, which is a genuine gap in completeness (the actor part of the claim matters less).
'Is defined' is not open to several readings; the real problem is that the format specification is missing, which is incompleteness, not ambiguity.
This is a verifiable performance limit (under 2 seconds); what happens when validation fails belongs to the functional credit-card requirements (e.g. GJ-021), not to this one.
'Malicious' has no criteria, so developers and testers cannot agree on what must be detected and rejected.
Calling a .kdb file a 'folder' plus the garbled 'of type the database can read' clause lets a reader take the rule as being about directories rather than files.
'Another usb drive' (a backup target) and the Yoggie 'USB system' (the host device) plausibly name different things, and GJ-043 uses 'usb drive' the same way, so there is no terminology conflict.

'Works in conjunction with' does not split responsibilities between mediator and PA, and PA is never expanded in the document, though in this goal-style CDN-peering document the roles may be clear to domain readers.
'No limits in length' is an explicit statement backed by a testable example (over 100 characters); the minimum-length question is a separate concern, not vagueness in this phrase.
The rule (a non-empty name is needed) is clear and testable; edge cases such as whitespace-only names are minor and would be incompleteness, not a vague term.
Nothing says which policies count as 'functional', so the requirement cannot be verified.
The 200 products per second figure makes the requirement measurable, and 'shall be able to' is standard capability wording, not a weak phrase.
Without a triggering event or a start and end point for the 1-second limit (sent or delivered), a tester cannot measure the requirement.
Saying the protocols 'are defined' without giving or referencing them leaves the requirement incomplete and unverifiable, even though the passive voice itself is minor.
In CDN peering, 'short-term' versus 'long-term' (PE-016) is probably a recognised category of arrangement rather than a time quantity that needs a number, so only domain knowledge can settle this.
Encrypting at rest can be checked as stated, but a security reviewer would normally ask for a minimum algorithm or key-strength standard, so the gap is defensible though partly a design matter.
This is mainly a measurable performance limit; failure handling belongs elsewhere, though the unclear start of the timing makes it slightly weaker than it looks.
Neither the plugins nor the meaning of 'interchangeable' (swapped at runtime, vendor-neutral, or sharing an API) is stated, so the requirement cannot be verified.
